How to Weave Plant Hangers for Indoor Greenery

Turn six palm leaf strips into a sturdy plant hanger that safely holds a 12 cm pot. Full measurements, knot-by-knot steps and honest fixes for the tricky parts.

11 February 2025 ME By Maya Ellis 8 min read 712 words
Share

On this page

  1. Why woven leaf hangers work indoors
  2. Weaving the hanger step by step
  3. Getting the balance right

In short

Turn six palm leaf strips into a sturdy plant hanger that safely holds a 12 cm pot. Full measurements, knot-by-knot steps and honest fixes for the tricky parts.

A woven plant hanger is the smallest project that still feels like real basketwork. It uses about six long strips, no base, and roughly ninety minutes of an evening, yet it lifts a plain windowsill into something people stop and photograph.

I make mine from fresh coconut or palm leaf strips cut about 1 cm wide. They are strong enough for a 12 cm terracotta pot with a light trailing plant, which weighs around 1.5 kg once watered. Anything heavier needs doubled strips and a firmer top knot.

The reason leaf hangers suit indoor greenery so well is that they breathe. A plastic or cord hanger traps moisture against the pot, but a leaf weave lets air move, so the compost dries more evenly and you see far fewer fungus gnats. They also age well: the strips darken to a warm honey colour after about six months in indirect light, and that patina is the point rather than a flaw.

Why woven leaf hangers work indoors

One rule separates a hanger that lasts five years from one that sags in a fortnight: the top loop must be a closed, load-bearing knot, not a decorative bow. Everything below it is just a tidy way of cradling the pot. Get the top right and the rest is forgiving; get it wrong and no amount of neat weaving will save it.

What You'll Need

  • 6 fresh palm or coconut leaf strips, each about 1 cm wide and 90 cm long
  • A 12 cm plant pot to size the cradle against
  • Sharp scissors
  • A metal ring about 4 cm across, or a doubled strip loop
  • A small peg or clip to hold strips while you work

Weaving the hanger step by step

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. 1

    Soften the strips

    Run each strip between your thumb and the back of a blunt knife to break the fibres, then soak them in warm water for ten minutes. They should bend into a full circle without cracking. If a strip snaps, it was too dry, so soak the rest a little longer.

  2. 2

    Anchor to the ring

    Fold all six strips in half over the 4 cm ring so twelve working ends hang down. Gather them and tie a single overhand knot about 3 cm below the ring to lock the bundle in place.

  3. 3

    Split into pairs

    Separate the twelve ends into six pairs. Cross the left strip of each pair over the right and tie a simple half knot, working around the ring so every knot sits at the same height.

  4. 4

    Build the cradle

    About 12 cm down, cross the outer strips of neighbouring pairs and knot them together to form a diamond mesh. Repeat 8 cm lower, then gather all the ends into one bundle.

  5. 5

    Test the fit

    Slip the 12 cm pot into the mesh and check the depth. The base of the pot should rest just above the final knot, not push through it. Adjust the middle row up or down by one knot if it sits wrong.

  6. 6

    Close and trim

    Tie all twelve ends in one firm overhand knot beneath the pot, then trim the tails to 4 cm and tuck them up into the weave so nothing dangles or unravels.

Getting the balance right

If the finished hanger leans, it is nearly always because the strips are uneven in width rather than because a knot is off-centre. Cut all six strips from the same leaf where you can, and hold them against each other before you start. When a pot still tilts, add one extra half knot on the short side to pull the cradle level.

Keep the first week gentle. The fibres settle as they dry, so re-tighten the top knot after seven days and trim any tails that have crept out of the weave. After that it holds its shape for years.

Helpful Tips

  • Keep the pot light: a 12 cm pot is the practical limit for single strips.
  • Water over a sink and let the pot drain before rehanging, so the weave never stays damp.
  • Re-tighten the top knot after the first week, once the fibres have settled.
  • In very dry rooms, mist the hanger now and then so the leaf does not turn brittle.

Frequently asked questions

How much weight can a woven leaf plant hanger hold?

A six-strip hanger made from 1 cm strips safely holds about 2 kg, which is roughly a 12 cm pot with damp compost and a small trailing plant. For heavier pots, double every strip and use two rings.

How long does a palm leaf plant hanger last?

Indoors and away from direct sun, expect two to three years before the strips stiffen. Misting it every few weeks in dry rooms keeps it flexible for longer.

Can I make a plant hanger from dried leaves?

Dried leaves crack when knotted. Soak dried strips in warm water for twenty minutes first, and they become pliable enough to knot without splitting.

Which plants suit a woven hanger best?

Light trailing plants such as pothos, string of pearls and small ferns. Avoid heavy succulents in large pots, which strain the mesh over time.
